C’est la veille de Noël, et avec les mes: It’s Christmas Eve, and with the government’s restrictions in place, big family dinners are nothing but a dream from 2019. It’s a hard time for everyone. But in the face of adversity, a new kind of love is emerging.
On vous présente donc quelques personnes: Here are a few people who are “putting their hearts on the barbecue.”
<strong>Une mère Noël à cœur ouvert</str: A Mrs. Claus with an open heart
Frigorifiée, Hanadi Saad, déguisée en mè: Freezing, Hanadi Saad, dressed as Mrs. Claus, dances to disco music as she waves to seniors standing on their balconies in a Brossard apartment building. She says she is worried about the second lockdown, planned from December 25 to January 11. The harsh winter and its lack of light will lead, she believes, to a rise in depression and in illnesses linked to weakened immune systems. Her organization, Justice Femme, has therefore put together a resource guide for seniors.
On y trouve une liste de centres d’écout: It includes a list of crisis lines and suicide prevention organizations, businesses that deliver groceries and tips for overcoming depression. In early December, she convinced two caterers and a pastry chef to prepare about thirty Christmas meals.
En ces 24 et 25 décembre, elle livre ces: On December 24 and 25, she is delivering these meals to families in need, to people who are alone or elderly, and to single mothers living in her neighbourhood. Behind her glasses, she struggles to hold back tears as she thinks about these residents’ loneliness, which is deepening this year with feelings of fear, anxiety and distress.
Originaire du Liban, Hanadi a fait des é: Originally from Lebanon, Hanadi studied in Quebec before founding the organization Justice Femme, shortly after the Parti québécois tried to legislate a ban on religious symbols in 2013. Since the start of the pandemic, the young forty-something has been trying to take concrete action to ease the anguish she feels about seniors dying of COVID-19 in our hospitals, CHSLDs and residences. “Why are they being sacrificed like this?” asks the woman whose name appears among the 25 most influential women in Canada. The pandemic has awakened painful memories for her.
Pendant 17 ans, elle a vécu dans un pays: For 17 years, she lived in a country torn apart by civil war. During the attacks carried out by Israel, she hid in underground tunnels to protect herself from the bombs. “We went from one region to another, as if we were refugees in our own country. I remember women running in the morning, wearing blood-soaked pyjamas,” she says.
Vingt-huit ans plus tard, l’image de mil: Twenty-eight years later, the image of thousands of seniors dying in Quebec, from loneliness, malnutrition or thirst, haunts her. “I feel like I’m living through a war. It gets to me. My childhood was stolen from me, but I started my adult life here, in peace, in well-being.”
Après plus d’une heure au grand froid, H: After more than an hour in the bitter cold, Hanadi continues her story. On Mother’s Day, with a handful of volunteers and a DJ, she got seniors dancing on the balconies of residences in disadvantaged neighbourhoods of Montréal and Laval. “I cried so much when I found out that a woman who couldn’t take being shut in any longer threw herself from the fifth floor of a residence in east Montréal,” she confides, wiping away a tear. Nearly 75% of older people have been left to fend for themselves since the start of the pandemic. At the worst of the crisis, some no longer had visits from nurses or social workers.
Les organismes membres du Regroupement d: Member organizations of the Regroupement des centres de prévention du suicide du Québec (RCPSQ) have received on average 20% more calls since the start of the pandemic. But it is hard to know whether the calls come as much from older people as from younger ones, says the Regroupement’s director, Linda Poirier.
À quelques rues de la demeure de Hanadi: A few streets from Hanadi’s home in Brossard, neighbours are helping each other too. Micheline, a 66-year-old retiree, decided to give some of her time. She took a two-metre stick to help her neighbour, who lives completely isolated. Every day, they walk together. “My neighbour lost her sight at 23, and she’s now 57.
Thanks to her, I’ve learned resilience. I admire her strength of character and, above all, she doesn’t let difficulties bring her down,” says Micheline.
La dame et son mari aident aussi des voi: She and her husband also help neighbours in their seventies carry their grocery bags and pick up their mail from their postal boxes. Small gestures that bring joy. “I feel a lot of gratitude, and we’re especially proud to help people who need it,” she says with a smile.
Hanadi Saad a-t-elle l’impression de cha: Does Hanadi Saad feel she is changing things? “Yes, maybe,” she answers. “If everyone did one small thing, we’d be living in the best of all worlds. You know what’s missing? Love. We live in a very individualistic and selfish world.” By bringing a meal to seniors and families in need, or by dancing for them outside in the freezing cold, Hanadi Saad feels filled with energy and strength. “I want to change the world,” she concludes in a convinced tone.
On peut participer à un changement, mais: We can take part in change, but we can also bring it about. We can influence it… that’s what leadership is.” She wants to grow old at home, like her 93-year-old grandmother, who receives CLSC services and help from her loved ones. “Take care of your seniors, because there are 1,001 ways to give them love, and not only in person,” she exclaims.
Mais si Hanadi Saad veut aider les aînés: But if Hanadi Saad wants to help seniors, there are also seniors who help young people. On the TikTok platform, <l1>the account Reste Pépé</l1>, run by three seniors named Gab, JR and Dan, was created “to encourage young people.” And it’s a huge hit! Through choreographies, sometimes set to rigodon, sometimes to hip-hop, and the latest trends on the platform, which is mainly used by young people, Reste Pépé encourages young people to get tested and to respect physical distancing, but also brings a wave of love to young people who lost a grandparent this year.
« J’ai perdu ma grand-mère cette année,: “I lost my grandmother this year, first Christmas without her, thank you for being there for me and making me smile again,” writes one young user. “This year, we lost both our grandmas to COVID, my eyes are full of tears seeing you! Thank you for being there,” adds another user.
<strong>Conseils aux aînés isolés (tirés: Tips for isolated seniors (taken from Justice Femme’s resource guide)
Sortir et s’exposer à la lumière naturel: Go outside and expose yourself to natural light. When feeling anxious, do different breathing exercises, but above all, repeat out loud: “Everything is going to be okay,” and think of all the people who love you. Listen to music, sing, take a hot bath. Also express your emotions to a friend or to family.
« En évacuant les tensions qui pèsent lo: “By letting go of the tension weighing heavily on your heart, you’ll feel much better,” the guide says.
Le guide de ressources de Justice Femme: Justice Femme’s resource guide is available on request to organizations, residences and people aged 55 and over.
